transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-04-11
Time: 16:00 PDT
Duration: 42m
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Raj Patel (Aphelion - Head of ML), Sofia Martinez (Aphelion - Platform Eng), Ethan Lee (Aphelion - CTO)

Summary (auto): Integration discovery for Redwood Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private. Topics: SDK integration, LangChain / LlamaIndex connectors, gateway/proxy pattern for multi-tenant routing, rate limits/quotas, observability hooks and traces. Customer concerned about on-prem latency, VPC peering, and enterprise audit logs.

Transcript:
[00:00:03] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya from Redwood, AE on this account, and with me is Liam O'Connor, our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:00:12] Raj: Good, thanks. Quick intro — I'm Raj, Head of ML at Aphelion. Sofia and Ethan are on as well.
[00:00:18] Sofia: Hi all.
[00:00:20] Ethan: Hey.
[00:00:30] Maya: Cool. The plan for today is to understand your integration needs — SDKs, any LangChain or LlamaIndex usage, where you'd run the gateway or proxy, and requirements around rate limits and observability. We'll go through options: Hosted API for quick start, Dedicated for predictability, and Private (VPC/on-prem) for compliance.
[00:00:50] Raj: Great. To start, high level — we're running a retrieval-augmented generation pipeline. We use LangChain in python, a mix of LlamaIndex for doc indexing, and we want the model serving to be as close to our infra as possible for latency. Also need fine-grained quotas per customer.
[00:01:05] Liam: Okay — that's helpful. A couple clarifying q's: 1) Are you using streaming responses today? 2) Typical sequence length and RAG doc size?
[00:01:15] Raj: We stream to our UI. Sequence lengths are usually 512 tokens for generation, retrieval adds another 2–3k tokens in the prompt. Concurrency peaks around 120 qps, but that's across many tenants.
[00:01:28] Sofia: And we need per-tenant rate limits — e.g., bronze/silver/gold tiers, but also hard safety caps.
[00:01:36] Maya: Got it. For SDKs we have official python and node SDKs, they support streaming, chunked responses and built-in retry/backoff. We also have examples for LangChain and LlamaIndex connectors. Liam, you want to call out the connector details?
[00:01:48] Liam: Sure. Our LangChain connector is basically an LLM wrapper that maps the LangChain LLM interface to Redwood's streaming and function-calling features — note there are sometimes name mismatches in the auto-transcripts, like people see 'Redwood Dedicated' as 'Redwood de-cided' in some notes. For LlamaIndex we have a direct client helper which handles chunking and embedded calls. The examples repo includes a small faststart app that wires RAG with caching.
[00:02:12] Raj: When you say caching — you mean prefix/KV cache at the runtime?
[00:02:16] Liam: Yes — we do prefix and KV cache to reduce repeated token decoding for hot prompts. That reduces cost and latency; it's configurable per deployment.
[00:02:24] Ethan: What's the integration pattern if we want to run our own gateway/proxy? We have an edge ingress that handles auth and tenant routing.
[00:02:32] Maya: Two common patterns: 1) Use Redwood as the backend and call the Hosted API through your proxy — you can add auth and tenant headers. We support per-request metadata so you can tag tenant_id. Rate limits and quotas can be enforced both client-side (your proxy) and server-side (Redwood per API key or per-tenant). 2) For Dedicated or Private, you can run the gateway alongside Redwood runtime inside your VPC and keep traffic internal — that's what many enterprise customers do.
[00:02:55] Sofia: If we run Dedicated behind our proxy, does Redwood still provide observability hooks? We want traces tied to our tracing system (Jaeger/Zipkin) and per-request tokens breakdown.
[00:03:06] Liam: Yes. We emit structured traces and logs — you can ship to your observability stack via OTLP, or we can provide a secure forwarding integration. Token-level cost and latency breakdowns are available in Redwood Console, and you can pull them via our metrics API. We also support trace ids in the response header so you can correlate.
[00:03:22] Raj: Security — KMS, SSO, audit logs, SOC2?
[00:03:26] Maya: Redwood Hosted is SOC2 compliant; we have enterprise add-ons for log retention and SSO/SAML, RBAC. Dedicated and Private give you more control: VPC peering, customer-managed KMS/HSM integrations, and audit logs stored in your environment. We'll send the security pack after the call.
[00:03:40] Ethan: On quotas — can we set per-route quotas and burst allowances?
[00:03:44] Liam: Yes — we support per-route, per-api-key quotas plus burst windows. You can define soft and hard limits, and attach policies: throttle, queue, or reject. There's also token-based billing so you can chargeback per-customer.
[00:03:58] Sofia: Is there a way to do canary rollouts or model version pinning per-tenant?
[00:04:02] Maya: Absolutely. Console supports model pinning per route and canary rollouts; you can do gradual traffic shifts, A/B comparisons, and automatic fallback policies if latency or error thresholds exceed SLOs.
[00:04:12] Raj: For LangChain/LlamaIndex we need code snippets. Can you show an example of calling the SDK with streaming and function-calls?
[00:04:19] Liam: I'll paste a snippet after the call — we have a python example that uses the Redwood SDK LLM class with stream=True, and another that wraps it into LangChain's AsyncLLM. LlamaIndex uses a 'RedwoodIndex' adapter in our examples. Note — some community forks call it 'Llama IDX' in docs, which is wrong, it's LlamaIndex.
[00:04:36] Ethan: Latency — if we do Hosted, what's typical 95th percentile for 512 tokens?
[00:04:40] Liam: Hosted for our curated models on standard regions is usually 95th %ile ~180–350ms per request for shorter contexts; with 512 generation + retrieval it will be higher — maybe 400–800ms depending on retrieval pre-processing. Dedicated can get you more predictable throughput and lower p95 because you reserve GPU pools. Private on-prem gives you the lowest network latency but depends on your hardware.
[00:05:05] Raj: For benchmarking, can we run a short test that simulates our traffic? We want to see cost change with batching and quantization.
[00:05:12] Maya: Yes — we can run a 30-minute benchmark on Dedicated with your sample prompts. We'll need a traffic profile and some sample documents. We'll then show cost/batching/quantization tradeoffs in the report.
[00:05:22] Sofia: About quantization — does Redwood support 4-bit q configs for transformer models? And do you provide recommendations per workload?
[00:05:29] Liam: Yes we support a range of quantization profiles; Redwood Optimize will recommend quantization and batching settings per workload. Some models are more sensitive to 4-bit; we include quality regressions check tied to prompt sets.
[00:05:40] Raj: How about SDK connection limits — we have many short-lived connections. Any best practices?
[00:05:45] Liam: Use connection pooling and keep-alive. For streaming clients, reuse connections and implement client-side concurrency caps. Our SDK has a connection pool config by default. If you're behind a proxy, make sure it supports websocket or HTTP/2 keep-alive depending on streaming method.
[00:06:02] Ethan: Do you support local embedding caches? We already run an embedding service for nearest-neighbors, want to avoid re-embedding duplicates.
[00:06:09] Maya: You can use your own embedding pipeline and store vectors in your store — Redwood won't force you to use ours. For deduping, we recommend caching layer at the application side; we also expose embedding calls via SDK for convenience.
[00:06:20] [00:06:20] Raj: A couple of compliance questions: data residency in EU, and deletion/retention policies.
[00:06:24] Maya: We support region pinning — Hosted can be provisioned in EU regions for data residency. Dedicated/Private give you full control over storage and retention; we can sign data processing agreements. We'll include the DPA and data retention options in the security pack.
[00:06:39] Sofia: Integration wise, how heavy is the change to our LangChain codebase?
[00:06:43] Liam: Minimal — usually a couple of lines to swap out the LLM class to Redwood's wrapper. There are also prebuilt chains in our examples. LlamaIndex adapter is also drop-in for most use cases, but you should run the evals.
[00:06:56] Raj: Questions about cost allocation — do you have token attribution per tenant?
[00:07:00] Maya: Yes — token-level attribution by tenant_id is available; we also export per-route cost metrics and have usage APIs for daily exports to your billing system.
[00:07:10] [00:07:10] Ethan: Any gotchas running behind a proxy? We had issues with timeouts and chunked transfer once.
[00:07:15] Liam: The main gotchas: ensure proxy supports streaming and forward headers; tune idle timeout to be longer than expected streaming sessions; support chunked transfer-encoding for streaming responses. We'll share a proxy checklist.
[00:07:30] Raj: If we want to do a Private deployment — what's the timeline and ops footprint?
[00:07:34] Maya: Private deployments take longer — typically 6–10 weeks for on-prem with HSM/KMS integrations, network firewall configs and air-gap considerations. Dedicated can be done faster, 2–4 weeks for reserved capacity. Hosted is immediate. Timeline depends on compliance gating and infra readiness.
[00:07:52] Sofia: Do you instrument the runtime to emit metric hooks for per-request latency buckets?
[00:07:57] Liam: Yes — runtime emits granular metrics: token decode time, kernel time, queue wait, KV cache hit rate. We push metrics to Prometheus/OTLP or export via our metrics API. These show up in Console per-model and per-route.
[00:08:10] Raj: We have MLOps concerns — we run canary evals and need model quality regressions tracked over time.
[00:08:15] Maya: Redwood Optimize includes quality monitoring; you can tie eval prompt sets and surface regression alerts. We can also integrate with your evaluation pipeline via webhooks.
[00:08:26] Ethan: Pricing question — how do you price Dedicated vs Hosted?
[00:08:30] Maya: Hosted is usage-based per token and embedding units. Dedicated is a reserved capacity contract (monthly/annual) with committed throughput and lower unit costs; Private is enterprise licensing plus support and on-prem infra. We'll provide a sample pricing spreadsheet for your expected QPS.
[00:08:44] Sofia: Our next steps: we want the SDK examples, Dedicated pricing, and a technical deep dive.
[00:08:50] Maya: We'll get those over. Liam, anything else to add?
[00:08:53] Liam: I'll include the LangChain and LlamaIndex sample repo links and a short gateway/proxy checklist. Also I'll mention nuances: function-calling semantics, streaming backpressure, and kv-cache tuning.
[00:09:05] Raj: Sounds good. One more small nit — do you have an example of per-tenant throttling policy?
[00:09:09] Liam: Yes — policy examples include token-rate limits, concurrent request caps, and burst windows. We can attach policies to tenant_id using our policy engine.
[00:09:19] Ethan: Great. If we like results, we'll likely start with a Dedicated pilot.
[00:09:24] Maya: Perfect. We'll send the follow-ups and schedule the deep-dive. Thanks everyone.
[00:09:30] Raj: Thanks.
[00:09:32] Sofia: Thanks all.
[00:09:34] Ethan: Bye.

(Transcription notes: occasional mis-hearings present; proper nouns sometimes mangled — e.g., 'KV cache' transcribed as 'K V cash' in earlier raw transcripts.)
